items.title: PhD position: Safe deployment of semi-autonomous AI in radiology
items.desc: Functiebeschrijving Every day, radiologists review hundreds of scans to find out whether a patient has cancer. The number of scans keeps growing, but the number of radiologists does not. AI can help. For prostate cancer, AI systems can now read MRI scans about as well as experienced radiologists. Yet today a radiologist still checks every scan, so the AI saves little time. That could change if AI were allowed to handle the clear-cut cases on its own, leaving radiologists more time for the difficult ones. But a hospital is not a static environment. New scanners are installed, scan settings […] ge and the patient population shifts over time. Each of these changes can make an AI system less accurate without anyone noticing. Radiologists who work with AI every day may also start to trust it more than they should. European law now requires hospitals and manufacturers to keep monitoring AI once it is in use, but nobody has yet shown how to do that reliably in practice. In this PhD project, funded by Stichting Hanarth Fonds, you will work out how to monitor AI safely in daily clinical practice, using prostate MRI as a starting point. You will: develop and validate statistical methods that detect drops in AI performance early, using a multicenter dataset of more than 10,000 prostate MRI examinations collected over twelve years; design and run an international reader study that measures how strongly AI advice influences radiologists; translate these findings into a monitoring protocol together with international experts, aligned with the EU AI Act; test the protocol prospectively in a multicenter study at UMCG and Radboudumc on more than 500 new examinations, in parallel with routine care; publish your work in international journals and present it at conferences, leading to a PhD thesis. items.desc: Job Description Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is an inherited retinal disease that progressively damages photoreceptors, the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision. Although new treatments, including gene therapies, are emerging, monitoring disease progression remains challenging because current clinical imaging techniques cannot always detect subtle changes in these cells. By combining adaptive optics imaging with Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) and microperimetry, the project will investigate how microscopic changes relate to retinal structure, visual function, and disease progression. The ultimate goal is to develop reliable imaging biomarkers to support disease monitoring and future clinical trials. As a PhD candidate, you will play a central role in this project, developing and validating AI and image analysis methods for detecting and characterising cone photoreceptors in diseased retinas. PhD 11 - Thermo-hygral-mechanical modelling and optimisation of dry-out and early-age behaviour in castable refractory linings
A 36 Months PhD starting in October 2026 and supervised between UMINHO (Portugal) and RHIM-Leoben (Austria)
PhD11 will develop and validate a thermo-hygro-mechanical finite element modelling framework for the dry-out of castable ladle linings, comparing natural and accelerated drying schedules. The project will instrument laboratory specimens, a biaxial press and a pilot ladle to monitor moisture transport, temperature and internal stress. It will model damage caused by pore pressure, early-age creep and microcracking, and assess how these phenomena influence later corrosion and degradation.
PhD11 is closely connected to PhD06, PhD14 and PhD15. Its thermo-hygro-mechanical modelling of dry-out and early-age behaviour provides inputs for digital twin development and operational decision support, while also benefiting from materials knowledge on binder systems and castable design. Its results are also relevant for sustainability and traceability by contributing drying-phase performance indicators.
